paragraphs.source_en: The concentration/dispersion pattern is known not only among the foragers but also among the modern African pastoralists. Groups of the semi-nomadic Salei Masai in Tanzania meet periodically in an initiation camp which is considered a holy place and it is known to everyone in the region2. Every seven years, the young men and their parents walk around 100km, travelling alongside the mountain considered to belong to God, until they reach the initiation camp which is prepared for the ritual many months beforehand. Here for five days several hundred boys meet to undertake the initiation ritual of which an important part is dancing, entering into trance facilitated by the use of toxic herbs, body painting and hair shaving. Masai believe this ceremony has happened there since time immemorial.

paragraphs.source_en: These examples show that although the San, the Touareg and the Masai are thousands of kilometres distant and they have different subsistence economies, they share the same pattern of grouping and socializing in special places. These groupings are always regular in time, related to specific purposes and preceded by a kind of pilgrimage. The destination and the way to it are considered to be dwellings of spirits and/or gods. Such a similar pattern may indicate a very ancient common base where the same tradition in distant regions may have the same origin possibly stretching to prehistoric times.
